items.title: Figure 2 question: a rope pulls a sled across level snow. Classify each force as contact or field.

question.html: A free-body diagram of the sled shows three forces: 𝐹<sup>rope</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>sled</sup> (forward), 𝐹<sup>snow</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>sled</sup> (the friction force, backward) and 𝐹<sup>Earth's</sup><sup> </sup><sup>mass</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>sled</sup> (down). Classify each force as a contact force or a field force.

body.html: A contact force needs the agent to touch the system. A field force acts across empty space.
The rope is tied to the sled, and the snow touches the runners, so both are contact forces. Gravity acts on the sled with no touching needed.

answer.html: 𝐹<sup>rope</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>sled</sup> is a contact force; 𝐹<sup>snow</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>sled</sup> (friction) is a contact force; 𝐹<sup>Earth's</sup><sup> </sup><sup>mass</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>sled</sup> (gravity) is a field force.

check.html: If the sled were lifted off the snow and the rope removed, only gravity would still act on it.

items.title: Get It? (Lesson 1, p. 86): Is the pull of a magnet on a steel nail a contact force or a field force? Is the tension in a string a contact force or a field force? What decides the difference?

body.html: The difference is whether the agent must touch the system.

answer.html: A magnet attracts a nail across a gap, so its pull is a field force. A string's tension is exerted by a string that touches the object, so it is a contact force. What decides it is whether the agent touches the system.

items.title: Get It? (Lesson 1, p. 87): A hockey puck slides east across the ice and slows down. In which direction does the net force on the puck point, and in which direction does the puck accelerate?

body.html: Newton's second law, 𝑎= 𝐹<sub>net</sub> / 𝑚. Mass is positive, so 𝑎 and 𝐹<sub>net</sub> point the same way. A slowing object has acceleration opposite to its velocity.
The velocity is east and the speed is decreasing, so the acceleration is west. The net force has the same direction as the acceleration.

answer.html: Both the net force and the acceleration point west (opposite to the puck's motion).

check.html: Friction from the ice, a backward force, is the force that slows the puck, so a westward net force makes sense.

items.title: Cause and Effect (CCC, p. 87): Plan a demonstration that shows that a net force on a 0.50-kg lab cart causes it to accelerate. Use forces of 0.25 N, 0.50 N and 0.75 N.

body.html: To show cause and effect, change only the net force, hold everything else fixed, and measure the acceleration each time. If the acceleration follows the force, the force is the cause. Work (a workable plan): 1. Place a low-friction cart (𝑚= 0.50 kg) on a level track with a motion sensor. Pull it with a spring scale held at a steady reading. 2. Zero net force: with no pull, or a pull balanced by an equal pull the other way, predict and observe 𝑎= 0. 3. Unbalanced cases: pull with 0.25 N, 0.50 N and 0.75 N. Predicted accelerations:

4. Plot 𝑎 against 𝐹<sub>net</sub>. The points should lie on a straight line through the origin with slope 1 / 𝑚= 2.0 (m/s<sup>2</sup>) / N. 5. Reverse the direction of the pull; the acceleration should reverse too.

answer.html: 𝑎= 0 when the force is balanced; with an unbalanced force the acceleration points the same way as the force and is proportional to it (0.50, 1.0 and 1.5 m/s² for 0.25, 0.50 and 0.75 N). Since the acceleration appears and disappears with the net force, the net force is the cause.

items.title: 1 (crate lowered at constant velocity)

body.html: Constant velocity means 𝑎= 0, so the net force is zero and the two forces must balance (Newton's first law).

System: the crate. Motion diagram: equally spaced dots going down, equal-length velocity arrows. Forces: 𝐹<sup>cable</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>crate</sup> (up) and 𝐹<sup>Earth's</sup><sup> </sup><sup>mass</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>crate</sup> (down), equal in length.

answer.html: System = crate; 𝑎= 0 and 𝐹<sup>net</sup> = 0. FBD: equal-length arrows, 𝐹<sup>cable</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>crate</sup> up and 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>crate</sup> down.

check.html: Equal arrows give zero net force, matching the equal dot spacing.

items.title: 2 (medicine ball pushed upward and speeding up, still in the hands)

body.html: The ball speeds up while moving upward, so 𝑎 and 𝐹<sub>net</sub> are upward: the hands push up harder than gravity pulls down.

System: the ball. Motion diagram: dots farther and farther apart going up, acceleration up. Forces: 𝐹<sup>hands</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup> (up, long) and 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup> (down, shorter).

answer.html: System = ball; 𝑎 and 𝐹<sup>net</sup> upward; 𝐹<sup>hands</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup> > 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup>.

check.html: The longer upward arrow gives a net upward force, as the upward acceleration requires.

items.title: 3 (ball rising after release)

body.html: After release, the only force (air resistance ignored) is gravity. The ball slows down because the downward acceleration is opposite its upward velocity.
Motion diagram: dots getting closer together going up; 𝑎 downward. Forces: only 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup>, down.

answer.html: System = ball; 𝐹<sup>net</sup> = 𝐹<sup>Earth's</sup><sup> </sup><sup>mass</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup>, downward; 𝑎 downward (equal to 𝑔).

check.html: The direction of 𝑎 and 𝐹<sub>net</sub> agree, and a downward 𝑎 slows an upward motion.

items.title: 4 (ball falling and speeding up)

body.html: Same single force (gravity), but now velocity and acceleration are both downward, so the ball speeds up.
Motion diagram: dots getting farther apart going down; 𝑎 downward. Forces: only 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup>, down.

answer.html: System = ball; 𝐹<sup>net</sup> = 𝐹<sup>Earth's</sup><sup> </sup><sup>mass</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup>, downward; 𝑎 downward.

check.html: The free-body diagram matches Problem 3, because gravity does not depend on whether the ball rises or falls.

items.title: 5 (Challenge: catching the ball and bringing it to rest)

body.html: The ball moves downward and slows to rest, so the acceleration is upward (opposite to the velocity). The net force must be upward, so the hands push up harder than gravity pulls down.

Motion diagram: dots getting closer together going down; 𝑎 upward. Forces: 𝐹<sup>hands</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup> (up, long) and 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup> (down, shorter).

answer.html: System = ball; 𝑎 and 𝐹<sup>net</sup> upward; 𝐹<sup>hands</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup> > 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup>.

check.html: Slowing down means the acceleration is opposite to the velocity, so an upward 𝑎 is correct.

items.title: Get It? (Lesson 1, p. 89): A cart of mass 0.40 kg is pulled by several different net forces, and a graph of its acceleration versus net force is made. Describe the graph, give its slope, and tell what happens to 𝑎 if the net force triples.

body.html: Newton's second law, 𝑎= 𝐹<sub>net</sub> / 𝑚, so 𝑎 is directly proportional to 𝐹<sub>net</sub> for fixed mass.
The graph is a straight line through the origin. The slope is

answer.html: The graph is a straight line through the origin with slope 1 / 𝑚= 2.5 (m/s<sup>2</sup>) / N. Tripling the net force triples the acceleration, which points in the direction of the net force.

check.html: A 1.0 N net force on 0.40 kg gives 2.5 m/s<sup>2</sup>, which is the slope.

items.title: Get It? (Lesson 1, p. 90): A wagon of fixed mass is pulled with some net force. How must the net force change to make its acceleration four times as large?

body.html: For fixed mass, 𝑎= 𝐹<sub>net</sub> / 𝑚, so 𝑎∝𝐹<sub>net</sub>.

answer.html: Increase the net force to four times its original value (mass unchanged).

check.html: If 𝐹<sub>net</sub> →4𝐹<sub>net</sub>, then 𝑎→4𝐹<sub>net</sub> / 𝑚= 4𝑎.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 6 (Newton's Second Law): A sailboat is pushed east by a 410 N wind force and a 275 N current force. Find the net horizontal force.

body.html: 𝐹<sub>1</sub> = 410 N, 𝐹<sub>2</sub> = 275 N, both east. Unknown: 𝐹<sub>net</sub>.
Forces are vectors. Forces along the same line in the same direction add.

answer.html: 685 N east.

check.html: The net force is larger than either force, as expected when both act the same way.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 7: Now the 410 N wind force pushes the sailboat east, but the 275 N current force pushes it west. Find the net force and its direction.

body.html: 410 N east, 275 N west. Unknown: 𝐹<sub>net</sub> and its direction.
Choose the direction of the larger force as positive; the other force is then negative.

answer.html: 135 N east (the direction of the larger force).

check.html: The net force is smaller than either force and points the way of the stronger one.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 8 (Challenge): Three children pull a wagon along a straight path. Imani pulls east with 28 N, Jorge pulls east with 37 N, and Lena pulls west with 71 N. Find the net force and explain how Newton's second law predicts the wagon's motion.

body.html: Take east as positive. Add the signed forces, then use 𝑎= 𝐹<sub>net</sub> / 𝑚.

The negative sign means the net force points west. Newton's second law says the wagon accelerates west with 𝑎= (6 N) / 𝑚 (the wagon's mass is not given, so the number cannot be computed). Only the unbalanced 6 N produces acceleration: Lena's 71 N pull westward cancels most of the 65 N eastward pull of the other two.

answer.html: 𝐹<sub>net</sub> = 6 N west. The wagon accelerates westward, 𝑎= (6 N) / 𝑚; it speeds up if it was moving west, or slows down if it was moving east.

check.html: 71 N −65 N = 6 N, smaller than Lena's pull and directed her way.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 9: A net force of 1.9 N acts on a 0.83-kg lab cart. Find its acceleration.

body.html: 𝐹<sub>net</sub> = 1.9 N, 𝑚= 0.83 kg. Unknown: 𝑎.
Newton's second law, 𝑎= 𝐹<sub>net</sub> / 𝑚.

answer.html: 𝑎= 2.3 m/s<sup>2</sup> in the direction of the net force.

check.html: 1 N / kg = 1 m/s<sup>2</sup>, and 1.9 divided by a number a bit below 1 is a bit more than 1.9.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 10: Omar (31.5 kg) sits on a sled on smooth ice. His father wants Omar to accelerate at 0.65 m/s2. What horizontal force must his father exert? (Ignore friction.)

body.html: 𝑚= 31.5 kg, 𝑎= 0.65 m/s<sup>2</sup>, no friction. Unknown: 𝐹.
With no resistance, the pull is the net force: 𝐹<sub>net</sub> = 𝑚𝑎.

answer.html: 𝐹= 20 N (20.475 N, rounded to two sig figs).

check.html: A 31.5 kg child weighs about 309 N; 0.65 / 9.8 ≈0.07 of that is about 20 N, so it is reasonable.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 11 (Challenge): A force of 395 N acts to the right and a force of 210 N acts to the left on a loaded sled. The sled starts from rest and reaches 7.5 m/s to the right after 4.0 s. (a) Draw the force diagram. (b) Find the net force. (c) Find the mass of the sled and load. (a) Force diagram

question.html: Take right as positive. The diagram has a dot (the sled) with an arrow proportional to 395 N pointing right, labeled 𝐹<sup>1</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>sled</sup>, and a shorter arrow proportional to 210 N pointing left, labeled 𝐹<sup>2</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>sled</sup>.

body.html: Find the acceleration from the motion, 𝑎= 𝛥𝑣/ 𝛥𝑡, then use 𝑚= 𝐹<sub>net</sub> / 𝑎.

answer.html: Two horizontal arrows from the sled: 395 N right (long) and 210 N left (shorter). The net force points right.
(b) 𝐹net = 185 N to the right.
(c) 𝑚≈99 kg (using the unrounded 𝑎= 1.875 m/s2).

check.html: A 99 kg load weighs about 970 N, and a net force of 185 N on it gives about 1.9 m/s<sup>2</sup>, which fits.

items.title: Figure 8 question: A curling stone is released and slides across a level sheet of ice until it stops. What forces eventually stop it?

body.html: By Newton's first law, the stone would keep moving at constant velocity if the net force on it were zero. It stops, so a net force opposing its motion must act.

Vertically, gravity down and the ice's upward normal force balance, so they cannot slow the stone. Horizontally, friction between the stone and the ice opposes the motion, and a small air resistance also opposes it.

answer.html: Friction between the stone and the ice (plus a small amount of air resistance) opposes the motion. Gravity and the normal force are balanced and do not change the stone's horizontal speed.

items.title: Lesson 1 Check Your Progress, Problem 12: Classify each item as (a) a contact force, (b) a field force, or (c) not a force: tension in a rope, the pull of a magnet on a nail, speed, the push of a table on a book, the pull of Earth on the Moon, velocity, air drag, volume.

body.html: A contact force needs touching; a field force acts at a distance; some things are properties or descriptions of motion, not forces.

Item Class Why tension in a rope a, contact force the rope touches the object pull of a magnet on a nail b, field force acts across a gap speed c, not a force describes how fast an object moves push of a table on a book a, contact force surfaces touch pull of Earth on the Moon b, field force gravity acts at a distance velocity c, not a force speed and direction of motion air drag a, contact force air touches the object volume c, not a force a property: the space the object occupies

answer.html: a (contact): tension, push of a table, air drag. b (field): magnet's pull, Earth's pull on the Moon. c (not a force): speed, velocity, volume.

items.title: Lesson 1 Check Your Progress, Problem 13: A box of books is hauled straight up on a rope, speeding up as it rises. Draw a free-body diagram of the box.

body.html: Speeding up while moving upward means upward acceleration, so the net force is upward: the rope's pull exceeds gravity.

System: the box (a dot). Up is positive. Forces: 𝐹<sup>rope</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>box</sup> (up, long) and 𝐹<sup>Earth's</sup><sup> </sup><sup>mass</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>box</sup> (down, shorter).

answer.html: System = box; two forces, 𝐹<sup>rope</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>box</sup> up (longer arrow) and 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>box</sup> down (shorter); 𝐹<sub>net</sub> and 𝑎 are upward.

items.title: Lesson 1 Check Your Progress, Problem 14: A bucket of sand is lowered down a mine shaft on a rope, speeding up as it descends. Draw a free-body diagram of the bucket.

body.html: The bucket moves down and speeds up, so 𝑎 is downward and 𝐹<sub>net</sub> is downward: gravity's pull exceeds the rope's pull.

System: the bucket with its sand. Forces: 𝐹<sup>rope</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>bucket</sup> (up, shorter) and 𝐹<sup>Earth's</sup><sup> </sup><sup>mass</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>bucket</sup> (down, longer), as in the right-hand diagram above.

answer.html: System = bucket; 𝐹<sup>rope</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>bucket</sup> up (shorter) and 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>bucket</sup> down (longer); net force and acceleration downward.

items.title: Lesson 1 Check Your Progress, Problem 15 (Critical Thinking): The same 3.0 N force is applied to cart A and then to cart B on a smooth track. Cart A accelerates at 1.2 m/s2 and cart B at 0.30 m/s2. Compare the masses, and find each mass.

body.html: 𝐹= 3.0 N, 𝑎<sub>𝐴</sub>= 1.2 m/s<sup>2</sup>, 𝑎<sub>𝐵</sub>= 0.30 m/s<sup>2</sup>.
𝑚= 𝐹<sub>net</sub> / 𝑎.

answer.html: Cart B has four times the mass of cart A (𝑚<sub>𝐴</sub>= 2.5 kg, 𝑚<sub>𝐵</sub>= 10 kg).

check.html: For the same force, the object with the smaller acceleration has the larger mass.

items.title: Figure 2 question: classify each force in the first panel

question.html: The first panel shows a hand pushing a book across a table. The free-body diagram shows three forces: 𝐹<sup>hand</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>book</sup>, 𝐹<sup>table</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>book</sup>, and 𝐹<sup>Earth's</sup><sup> </sup><sup>mass</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>book</sup>.

body.html: A contact force needs the agent to touch the system. A field force acts across empty space.
The hand touches the book, and the table touches the book, so both are contact forces. Earth's gravity acts on the book without needing to touch it.

answer.html: 𝐹<sup>hand</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>book</sup> is a contact force; 𝐹<sup>table</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>book</sup> (the normal force) is a contact force; 𝐹<sup>Earth's</sup><sup> </sup><sup>mass</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>book</sup> (gravity) is a field force.

check.html: Gravity is the only field force the book considers in this module, and it is the only one of the three that would still act if the book were lifted off the table.

items.title: Get It? (Lesson 1, p. 86): contact versus field forces

body.html: The difference is whether the agent must touch the system.

answer.html: A contact force is exerted by an agent that is touching the system (a push, a pull from a string, the table's support). A field force, such as gravity, is exerted with no contact between the agent and the system.

items.title: Get It? (Lesson 1, p. 87): direction of acceleration versus direction of net force

body.html: Newton's second law, 𝑎= 𝐹<sub>net</sub> / 𝑚. Mass is a positive number, so 𝑎 and 𝐹<sub>net</sub> must have the same sign.

answer.html: The acceleration always points in the same direction as the unbalanced (net) force.

check.html: In Figure 3 the falling ball accelerates downward and its net force is downward.

items.title: Cause and Effect (CCC, p. 87): plan a demonstration

body.html: To show cause and effect, change only the force imbalance, keep everything else fixed, and measure the acceleration each time. Repeating at several imbalances shows the acceleration follows the imbalance and is not just a coincidence. Work (a workable plan): 1. Put a low-friction cart (mass 𝑚 fixed) on a level track. Tie a string to each end, run each string over a pulley, and hang a known weight from each. Use a motion sensor (or video) to measure the cart's acceleration. 2. Balanced case: hang equal weights, for example 1.0 N on each side. Predict and observe 𝑎= 0 (the cart stays at rest or keeps a constant velocity). 3. Unbalanced cases: keep the left pull at 1.0 N and increase the right pull to 1.5 N, 2.0 N, 3.0 N. The net forces are 0.5 N, 1.0 N, 2.0 N, toward the larger pull. 4. Plot acceleration against net force. The points should lie on a straight line through the origin with slope 1 / 𝑚 (the cart plus hanging masses must be counted when they are part of the system; for a quick demonstration, use a spring scale on each side instead). 5. Repeat with the same net force made from different pairs of forces (for example 2.0 N vs 1.0 N and 3.0 N vs 2.0 N). The acceleration should be the same, which shows that only the difference matters. 6. Reverse the stronger side to show the acceleration reverses direction.

answer.html: 𝑎= 0 when the forces are balanced; when unbalanced, 𝑎 is directly proportional to the net force and points in the direction of the larger force, no matter how large the individual forces are. Because the acceleration disappears when the imbalance is removed and returns when it is restored, the imbalance is the cause.

items.title: 1 (skydiver falling at constant velocity)

body.html: Constant velocity means 𝑎= 0, so (Newton's first law) the net force is zero and the two forces must balance.

System: the skydiver. Motion diagram: equally spaced dots (downward), equal-length velocity arrows. Forces: 𝐹<sup>Earth's</sup><sup> </sup><sup>mass</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>diver</sup> (weight, downward) and 𝐹<sup>air</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>diver</sup> (drag, upward), equal in length.

answer.html: System = skydiver; 𝑎= 0 and 𝐹<sup>net</sup> = 0. FBD: equal-length arrows, 𝐹<sup>air</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>diver</sup> up and 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>diver</sup> down.

check.html: Equal arrows give zero net force, consistent with equal dot spacing.

items.title: 2 (softball tossed upward, still in the hand)

body.html: The ball speeds up while moving upward, so 𝑎 and 𝐹<sub>net</sub> are upward. The hand must push up harder than gravity pulls down.

System: the softball. Motion diagram: dots farther and farther apart going upward (velocity arrows growing), acceleration up. Forces: 𝐹<sup>hand</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup> (up, long) and 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup> (down, shorter).

answer.html: System = ball; 𝑎 upward, 𝐹<sup>net</sup> upward; 𝐹<sup>hand</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup> > 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup>.

check.html: The longer upward arrow means a net upward force, matching the upward acceleration.

items.title: 3 (softball rising after leaving the hand)

body.html: Once the ball leaves the hand, the only force (ignoring air resistance) is gravity. The ball slows down because the acceleration (downward) is opposite its velocity (upward).
System: the ball. Motion diagram: dots getting closer together going upward; 𝑎 points downward. Forces: only 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup>, downward.

answer.html: System = ball; 𝐹<sup>net</sup> = 𝐹<sup>Earth's</sup><sup> </sup><sup>mass</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup>, downward; 𝑎 downward (equal to 𝑔).

check.html: Direction of 𝑎 and 𝐹<sub>net</sub> agree, and a downward 𝑎 slows an upward motion.

items.title: 4 (softball falling and speeding up)

body.html: Same single force (gravity), but now velocity and acceleration are both downward, so the ball speeds up.
Motion diagram: dots getting farther apart going downward; 𝑎 downward. Forces: only 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup>, downward.

answer.html: System = ball; 𝐹<sup>net</sup> = 𝐹<sup>Earth's</sup><sup> </sup><sup>mass</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup>, downward; 𝑎 downward.

check.html: The free-body diagram is identical to Problem 3, because the force does not depend on whether the ball is rising or falling.

items.title: 5 (Challenge: catching the ball and bringing it to rest)

body.html: The ball moves downward and slows to rest, so the acceleration is upward (opposite to the velocity). The net force must be upward, so the hand pushes up harder than gravity pulls down.

Motion diagram: dots getting closer together going downward; 𝑎 upward. Forces: 𝐹<sup>hand</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup> (up, long) and 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup> (down, shorter).

answer.html: System = ball; 𝑎 and 𝐹<sup>net</sup> upward; 𝐹<sup>hand</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup> > 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>ball</sup>.

check.html: An object that slows down has acceleration opposite to its velocity, so the upward 𝑎 is right.

items.title: Get It? (Lesson 1, p. 89): relationship between net force and acceleration

answer.html: They are directly proportional (a straight line through the origin on an acceleration-force graph): doubling the net force doubles the acceleration, and the acceleration is in the direction of the net force. The slope of the line is 1 / 𝑚.

items.title: Get It? (Lesson 1, p. 90): changing the force to halve the acceleration

body.html: For a fixed mass, 𝑎= 𝐹<sub>net</sub> / 𝑚, so 𝑎∝𝐹<sub>net</sub>.

answer.html: Reduce the net force to one-half of its original value (mass unchanged).

check.html: If 𝐹<sub>net</sub> →𝐹<sub>net</sub> / 2, then 𝑎→(𝐹<sub>net</sub> / 2) / 𝑚= 𝑎/ 2.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 6 (Newton's Second Law): two forces in the same direction

question.html: Two horizontal forces, 225 N and 165 N, act on a canoe in the same direction. Find the net horizontal force.

body.html: 𝐹<sub>1</sub> = 225 N, 𝐹<sub>2</sub> = 165 N, same direction. Unknown: 𝐹<sub>net</sub>.
Forces are vectors. Forces along the same line in the same direction add.

answer.html: 390 N in the direction of the two forces.

check.html: The net force is larger than either force, as expected when they pull the same way.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 7: the same forces in opposite directions

body.html: 225 N one way, 165 N the opposite way. Unknown: 𝐹<sub>net</sub> and its direction.
Choose the direction of the larger force as positive; the other force is then negative.

answer.html: 60 N in the direction of the larger (225 N) force.

check.html: The net force is smaller than either force, and it has the direction of the stronger force.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 8 (Challenge): three sled dogs

question.html: Alutia pulls east with 35 N, Seward east with 42 N, Kodiak west with 53 N. Find the net force and explain how Newton's second law predicts the sled's motion.

body.html: Take east as positive. Add the signed forces, then use 𝑎= 𝐹<sub>net</sub> / 𝑚.

A positive result means eastward. Newton's second law then says the sled accelerates in that direction with 𝑎= 𝐹<sub>net</sub> / 𝑚= (24 N) / 𝑚 (the mass of the sled and load is not given, so the acceleration cannot be computed). The bigger the sled's mass, the smaller this acceleration. Notice that the dogs' pulls are not just "cancelled out": only the unbalanced 24 N produces acceleration; the 53 N westward pull simply reduces the effect of the 77 N eastward pull.

answer.html: 𝐹<sub>net</sub> = 24 N east. The sled accelerates eastward, 𝑎= (24 N) / 𝑚, i.e. it speeds up (or slows down, if it was moving west) in the direction of the net force.

check.html: 77 N −53 N = 24 N, a net force smaller than the total east pull and directed east.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 9 (Example Problem 1 practice): acceleration of a cart

question.html: A net force of 2.7 N acts on a 0.64-kg cart. Find 𝑎.

body.html: 𝐹<sub>net</sub> = 2.7 N, 𝑚= 0.64 kg. Unknown: 𝑎.
Newton's second law, 𝑎= 𝐹<sub>net</sub> / 𝑚.

answer.html: 𝑎= 4.2 m/s<sup>2</sup> in the direction of the net force.

check.html: 1 N / kg = 1 m/s<sup>2</sup>, and 2.7 divided by a number a bit less than 1 is a bit bigger than 2.7.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 10: pulling Kamaria

question.html: Kamaria (27.2 kg) wants 𝑎= 0.80 m/s<sup>2</sup> on ice. What force must her mother exert?

body.html: 𝑚= 27.2 kg, 𝑎= 0.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>, no friction. Unknown: 𝐹.
With no resistance the pull is the net force: 𝐹<sub>net</sub> = 𝑚𝑎.

answer.html: 𝐹= 22 N (21.76 N, rounded to two sig figs).

check.html: About one-tenth of a 27 kg child's weight (about 267 N) gives about 0.1 𝑔, so 0.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> is reasonable.

items.title: Lesson 1, Practice Problem 11 (Challenge): the crate

question.html: A 317 N force acts to the right and a 173 N force acts to the left. The crate starts from rest and reaches 6.5 m/s to the right after 5 s.

body.html: Take right as positive. The diagram has a dot (the crate) with an arrow of length proportional to 317 N pointing right, labeled 𝐹<sup>1</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>crate</sup>, and a shorter arrow proportional to 173 N pointing left, labeled 𝐹<sup>2</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>crate</sup>.
Find the acceleration from the motion, 𝑎= 𝛥𝑣/ 𝛥𝑡, then use 𝑚= 𝐹<sub>net</sub> / 𝑎.

answer.html: (a) Two horizontal arrows from the crate: 317 N right (long) and 173 N left (short). The net force points right.
(b) 𝐹net = 144 N to the right.
(c) 𝑚≈1.1 × 102 kg (about 111 kg).

check.html: A "large crate" of about 110 kg (weight about 1090 N) needs only 144 N net to reach about 1.3 m/s², which fits.

items.title: Figure 8 question: what forces eventually stop the block?

body.html: By Newton's first law the block would move at constant velocity forever if the net force on it were zero. It must stop, so a net force opposing its motion must act.

After leaving the car the block is in the air. Gravity pulls it down onto the floor, and air resistance (drag) opposes its forward motion a little. Once on the floor, friction between the block and the floor opposes its motion until it stops.

answer.html: Friction between the block and the floor (plus a small amount of air resistance); gravity makes the block fall to the floor where the friction acts.

items.title: Lesson 1 Check Your Progress, Problem 12: classify forces

body.html: A contact force needs touching; a field force acts at a distance; some things are not forces at all (properties or results).

Item Class Why mass c, not a force a property of an object (amount of matter) inertia c, not a force a property: resistance to changes in velocity push of a hand a, contact force hand touches the object friction a, contact force surfaces touch air resistance a, contact force air touches the object spring force a, contact force spring touches the object gravity b, field force acts without touching acceleration c, not a force a result of a net force, not a force

answer.html: a (contact): push of a hand, friction, air resistance, spring force. b (field): gravity. c (not a force): mass, inertia, acceleration.

items.title: Lesson 1 Check Your Progress, Problem 13: bag of sugar lifted at increasing speed

body.html: Speeding up while moving upward means upward acceleration, so the net force is upward: the hand's push exceeds gravity.

System: the bag of sugar (a dot). Up is positive. Forces: 𝐹<sup>hand</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>sugar</sup> (up, long), 𝐹<sup>Earth's</sup><sup> </sup><sup>mass</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>sugar</sup> (down, shorter).

answer.html: System = bag of sugar; two forces, 𝐹<sup>hand</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>sugar</sup> up (longer arrow) and 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>sugar</sup> down (shorter); 𝐹<sub>net</sub> and 𝑎 are upward.

items.title: Lesson 1 Check Your Progress, Problem 14: water bucket lifted at decreasing speed

body.html: The bucket moves upward but slows, so 𝑎 is downward and 𝐹<sub>net</sub> is downward: the rope's pull is less than the bucket's weight.

System: the bucket (with its water). Forces: 𝐹<sup>rope</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>bucket</sup> (up, shorter) and 𝐹<sup>Earth's</sup><sup> </sup><sup>mass</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>bucket</sup> (down, longer), as drawn in the right-hand diagram above.

answer.html: System = bucket; 𝐹<sup>rope</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>bucket</sup> up (shorter) and 𝐹<sup>Earth</sup><sup> </sup><sup>on</sup><sup> </sup><sup>bucket</sup> down (longer); net force and acceleration downward.

items.title: Lesson 1 Check Your Progress, Problem 15 (Critical Thinking): two blocks, same force

body.html: The same 1 N force on block 1 gives acceleration 𝑎<sub>1</sub>; on block 2 it gives 𝑎<sub>2</sub> = 3𝑎<sub>1</sub>.
𝑚= 𝐹<sub>net</sub> / 𝑎.

answer.html: The second block has one-third the mass of the first (the first block is three times as massive).

check.html: For the same force, the object with the greater acceleration has the smaller mass.
